claims.text: Thermal annealing of a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy induces intermetallic precipitation.
The annealing-induced intermetallic precipitates are Mg-rich.
Growth of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates alters the local composition of the matrix.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitation sequesters active Mg from the matrix.
Sequestering Mg from the matrix reduces local galvanic coupling.
Galvanic coupling involving available matrix Mg drives rapid localized corrosion.
Annealing-enabled Mg sequestration promotes formation of a more coherent and protective oxide layer during high-temperature oxidation.
Annealed samples will have lower corrosion rates than as-cast samples.
Annealed samples will develop more protective high-temperature oxide scales than as-cast samples.
The proposed initial alloy has a density below 6 g/cm³.
The as-cast initial alloy contains metastable solid solutions.
The as-cast initial alloy contains minor pre-existing intermetallic phases.
Annealing at approximately 300–500 °C can promote partial precipitation without complete homogenization.
The as-cast baseline has more available Mg than the annealed state.
The greater availability of Mg in the as-cast state produces higher galvanic activity.
The greater availability of Mg in the as-cast state results in less effective oxide formation.
The proposed mechanism applies broadly to Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys below 6 g/cm³ under moderate annealing conditions.
Compositions or processing conditions that prevent measurable intermetallic precipitation may not produce the predicted corrosion and oxidation behavior.
